title: Forecasting the Language Distribution
award_status: MCM outstanding paper in the supplied 2018 special-award corpus

source.relative_path: 2018美赛特等奖/B题5篇/B91566-Forecasting the Language Distribution.pdf

source_quality.notes: All 26 physical pages were read and visually reviewed through five byte-bounded page contact sheets and three focused formula sheets. Ordinary text extraction omits display-equation glyphs, so equations 11, 12, 15, 16, and 20 retain medium-confidence or dependency-only normalization. The extraction-only commercial watermark and running team header are excluded from author evidence.

context_sources: summary, COO memo, full report body, references, and Tables A1-A8
language, population, tourism, trade, media, migration, and city-classification sources cited by the paper

task_reconstruction.summary: Forecast worldwide and country-level distributions of major language speakers for fifty years, determine office locations and working languages from the forecast, discuss long-run office viability, and communicate conditional advice to a COO.
inputs: 2014-2017 native and total speaker observations for 26 selected languages
official-language, tourism, trade, technology-time, and social-media proxies
city classification plus illustrative multilingual hiring cost C and benefit F premises
outputs: 2068 native-speaker and total-speaker quantities, proportions, and ranks
2018 and 2068 country-language arrays and English distribution maps
six office cities, optimal employee language counts, and working-language sets
capacity, input-disruption, and fitted-parameter sensitivity evidence plus COO memo

assumptions.summary: Languages with more than 50 million speakers are represented by a fixed 26-language state set.
Thirty-six countries selected by population, GDP, and data availability stand in for the geographic system.
The official-language support ratio is treated as time-invariant during the observation and forecast windows.
Country language proportions are approximated by 2015 values when allocating tourism and trade exposure.
The worldwide carrying capacity is fixed at 11 billion while multilingual speaker stocks may overlap.
A shared maximum transition-rate interface is used when generalizing the cited bilingual mechanism.
Each country carrying capacity is fixed at 1.5 times its 2016 population before later sensitivity variants.
Historical mean tourism and trade relationships are held fixed in the domestic resistance interface.
Mean historical country-to-country migration rates are extended into the future without route-level uncertainty.
Migrants retain the origin country's language composition when flows are allocated across languages.
The illustrative office calculation sets C and F to ten percent, requires at least two employee languages, and requires English among them.
Long-run office viability is discussed conditionally because salary, benefit, technology, efficiency, and communication-cost data are unavailable.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Worldwide native-speaker and additional-language counts for 26 selected languages are retained separately for 2014-2017.
Official-language support is operationalized as the number of recognizing countries divided by a declared world-country denominator of 197.
Outbound tourist totals are allocated to languages through country-level speaker proportions, with 2015 shares used as an approximation.
Absolute imports plus exports are allocated to languages to construct the declared international-business exposure index.
Facebook language-learning group participation is used as the paper's social-media proxy, with query and sampling details absent.
Country populations and 2016 baselines feed domestic growth, shares, and the assumed country carrying capacities.
Domestic tourism and trade interfaces are averaged over 2000-2016 before entering the country-language resistance term.
United Nations migration observations from 1991-2017 at nominal five-year intervals feed route-rate estimation.
Country-language speaker proportions allocate route migration to language-specific emigrant and immigrant stocks.
Annual observed language-stock changes over 2014-2017 are the stated response used by the gradient-descent fitting procedure.
The 2018 and simulated 2068 country-language arrays are the stated inputs to language-wise and country-wise ANOVA tables.
Table 2 binds six selected cities to an optimal language count and a corresponding working-language set.
Tables A1-A2 freeze the selected 36-country and 26-language state universes used by the coupled model.
Table A8 supplies the external 2016 city classification consumed after the language-economics screen.

models.summary: MU-B-2018-91566-001: Represent two language-community shares as opposing transition flows before extending the mechanism.
MU-B-2018-91566-002: Map target-language share and status, moderated by resistance and a maximum rate, into directional shift probability.
MU-B-2018-91566-003: Add density-limited natural reproduction to language-community dynamics.
MU-B-2018-91566-004: Construct official-language, tourism, and trade indices that feed status and resistance.
MU-B-2018-91566-005: Update every worldwide language stock using incoming shifts, outgoing shifts, and density-limited global population growth.
MU-B-2018-91566-006: Generalize the cited shift probability from two communities to each ordered language pair.
MU-B-2018-91566-007: Turn tourism, trade, technology, media, and official-language support into time-varying resistance and status inputs.
MU-B-2018-91566-008: Apply worldwide competition and population growth to each language within each country.
MU-B-2018-91566-009: Replace worldwide policy, tourism, trade, and resistance inputs with country-language counterparts and historical means.
MU-B-2018-91566-010: Estimate a country-to-country annual migration rate from five-year net migration and hold its historical mean into the future.
MU-B-2018-91566-011: Move country-language stocks along fixed migration rates while adding local natural growth.
MU-B-2018-91566-012: Combine domestic language competition, country population growth, and cross-country migration in one country-language update.
MU-B-2018-91566-013: Fit unknown competition, resistance, status, and growth parameters to 2014-2017 annual language-stock changes.
MU-B-2018-91566-014: Advance population and language states to 2068 under a discrete carrying-capacity law.
MU-B-2018-91566-015: Compare 2018 and 2068 language and country output arrays to support a geographic-stability statement.
MU-B-2018-91566-016: Choose the number of languages per employee and screen office countries using local language shares, unit return, and marginal language cost.
MU-B-2018-91566-017: Probe three uncertainty sources using capacity multipliers, country-language swaps, and changes in resistance, status, and maximum shift rate.

results_trace.summary: The paper reports completion of gradient-descent parameter fitting, but the extracted text does not expose a reproducible numeric parameter ledger.
Figures 3-4 separately report simulated 2068 native-speaker and total-speaker quantities after a fifty-year run.
Figures 5-6 separately report simulated 2068 native-speaker and total-speaker proportions.
Figures 7-8 report top-fifteen ranks for native and total speakers rather than only the top ten.
Wu Chinese replaces Punjabi in the reported native-speaker top ten and replaces French in the total-speaker top ten.
Language-wise ANOVA reports Malay as the exception; the paper attributes this to Malay's aggregated definition and inaccurate data.
Country-wise ANOVA is used to support a limited statement about differences between the 2018 and simulated 2068 arrays.
Figures 9-10 provide English country distributions at baseline and horizon as a concrete geographic comparison.
The illustrative office screen selects Paris, Tokyo, Milan, Toronto, Bombay, and Brussels with two or three working languages each.
The paper declines to determine long-run office viability without exact cost, benefit, salary, technology, and communication-efficiency data.
Capacity scenarios q=1.25, 1.75, and 2 are reported as not materially changing the tested quantity and proportion arrays under the paper's ANOVA analysis.
Twenty one-country language-distribution swaps are reported as producing no significant aggregate model difference.
The Australia case is reported as comparatively insensitive to resistance, status, and negative c changes but sensitive to positive increases in c.
The paper presents multi-language competition plus migration coupling as more practical and interpretable than the cited bilingual baseline.
The source claims forecast access by country, language, and year, while code, uncertainty, and external forecast validation remain absent.
The conclusion reassembles fitted competition, migration, country initialization, fifty-year forecasts, and the economic hiring screen.

contributions.summary: Retains a cited directional competition baseline before identifying the demographic and multilingual mechanisms required by the task.
Operationalizes government support, tourism, trade, technology, and media before combining them in status and resistance.
Generalizes language shift to a 26-language worldwide stock balance with separate transition and demographic contributions.
Adapts the worldwide interface to country-language states and distinguishes domestic policy and historical-mean proxies.
Keeps migration as a country-to-country population transfer rather than silently relabeling it as language conversion.
Presents one geographic recurrence with domestic shift, population growth, emigration, and immigration visible as separate terms.
Turns local language coverage into a marginal hiring-benefit screen before applying an external city hierarchy.
Refuses an exact long-run office conclusion until company-specific cost, benefit, salary, technology, and communication data are available.
States data and parameter-fitting weaknesses before proposing more data, parameter reduction, and future-statistics evaluation.

writing_logic.summary: The summary starts from geographic language shift and an office decision, then previews worldwide, domestic, geographic, fitting, forecast, sensitivity, and recommendation stages in dependency order.
The introduction separates temporal speaker forecasting, country distribution, and office choice before attributing the bilingual competition mechanism that will be extended.
Problem analysis turns policy, tourism, trade, technology, and media from a qualitative inventory into status or resistance interfaces before the governing equations appear.
Model construction moves from worldwide multi-language balance to domestic adaptation, route migration, and a single country-language geographic recurrence.
The fitting algorithm aligns observed and predicted annual changes, then hands fitted parameters to fifty-year worldwide and geographic simulations.
Results progress from quantities to shares and ranks, then from country-language arrays to ANOVA, English maps, and the marginal employee-language decision.
The office table is followed by an explicit missing-company-data boundary, three sensitivity families, source-acknowledged weaknesses, future work, and a conclusion that reassembles the chain.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The summary's full model-staircase-to-office route is judge-scannable, but award status alone does not prove that this structure caused the outcome.

The worldwide schematic and separated shift, status, resistance, and growth interfaces make the mechanism inspectable before simulation, a plausible clarity advantage rather than demonstrated judge causation.
The quantity-share-rank sequence and paired English maps support rapid comparison, subject to missing uncertainty and chart-value reconstruction.
The office table followed by a missing-data boundary closes the stakeholder loop without pretending to know unavailable long-run company economics.

weaknesses.summary: Equation 11 is rasterized; tourism, trade, media, time trend, and reference resistance are visible dependencies, but exact operators, signs, scaling, and coefficients cannot be recovered reliably and are retained as f_11.
Equation 12 is transcribed at medium confidence as official-language support times a status scale plus a baseline; the raster and missing parameter ledger prevent stronger glyph and scale claims.
Equation 15 is rasterized; its country tourism, trade-to-GDP, media, time, and reference-resistance inputs are retained, but unresolved operators remain explicitly represented by f_15.
Equation 16 is retained at medium confidence as the domestic official-language indicator scaled into status plus a baseline; exact glyph and coefficient evidence is incomplete.

Equation 20 substitutes historical tourism and trade means into domestic resistance, but its rasterized combination cannot be normalized beyond the confirmed f_20 dependency interface without inventing operators.

Equation 21 divides every migration interval by five years although the stated 1991-2017 series includes a final interval that may not be five years; route timing, signs, and averaging weights require source-table reconciliation.

Equation 27 combines domestic shift, demographic growth, and migration, but global and country-language speaker stocks may overlap and are fitted at different aggregation levels; conservation and cross-level reconciliation are unproved.

Equation 29 mixes a language-covered population share, a benefit factor F, and per-language cost C; the paper's illustrative C=F=10 percent does not establish compatible currency units or city-specific economics.
The authors state that limited linguistic data forced simplification, including a common maximum transfer speed between languages.
The authors state that manual derivation, many fitted parameters, and long fitting time burden the gradient-descent procedure.

independent_extensions.summary: Freeze every language count, source definition, reference year, multilingual-overlap rule, country allocation, and proxy query in a source-to-variable ledger.
Recover equations 11, 12, 15, 16, and 20 from author source or higher-fidelity formula evidence, then test signs, units, monotonicity, and probability bounds.
Replace fixed mean net migration with a versioned origin-destination process that handles interval length, route direction, uncertainty, and conservation explicitly.
Publish the fitted parameter vector, objective, gradients, initialization, scaling, bounds, convergence trace, residuals, and held-out forecast design.
Replace baseline-versus-simulation ANOVA proof language with direct distribution distances, effect sizes, multiple-test control, and future held-out observations.
Estimate city-specific revenue, employee counts, salary premiums, communication cost, existing offices, budget, and uncertainty before optimizing a portfolio.
Run joint parameter, input, structural, horizon, and decision-level sensitivity so uncertainty reaches n-star and the six-city recommendation.
Use later country-language observations for external validation and compare simplified versus reduced-parameter alternatives under a preregistered error metric.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: bind stable, insensitive, best, suitable, economical, and prove claims to the exact response, comparator, horizon, perturbation, statistical test, and unresolved uncertainty

ledger every language stock, country share, tourist and trade allocation, media query, population, capacity, migration route, parameter response, city class, unit, year, transformation, and downstream consumer
combine competition, natural growth, domestic proxy adaptation, and migration only through typed country-language increments before handing forecasts to geography and office decisions
keep people, overlapping speaker stocks, shares, transition probabilities, changes, ranks, ANOVA outputs, net benefit, optimal language count, and city portfolio as distinct outputs

replace broad stability language with held-out forecast error, conservation, direct distribution distance, multiple-test control, joint parameter and structural uncertainty, and final office-portfolio stability

preflight raster glyph confidence, variable closure, percent-versus-fraction scale, carrying-capacity units, migration interval length, aggregation reconciliation, C/F dimensions, and probability or nonnegativity bounds
turn language-shift schematics and country maps into auditable mechanism and comparison views with units, arrow semantics, scales, numeric alternatives, horizon, uncertainty, and text descriptions

trace every requested output from selected language/country states through worldwide competition, domestic adaptation, migration coupling, fitting, fifty-year forecasts, geographic checks, marginal hiring economics, and the COO memo

unresolved_questions: Which exact Ethnologue definitions, editions, proficiency thresholds, and reference dates produced native and total speaker counts for 2014-2017?
How are multilingual people represented when the sum of language-speaker stocks exceeds population?
Which 36 countries were excluded for missing data, and how do population and GDP criteria combine with data availability?
What exact country-language table and normalization allocate tourism and trade quantities, including missing and multilingual shares?
What Facebook queries, dates, groups, duplicate controls, and participant definitions construct D_l and D_i_l?
What exact operators, coefficients, signs, transformations, and units appear in rasterized equations 11, 15, and 20?
What status scales and baselines are authoritative for equations 12 and 16?
How are pairwise transition probabilities normalized or bounded when each target may receive shifts from 25 source languages?
Why is global K fixed at 11 billion and each K_i at 1.5 times 2016 population when language-speaker stocks overlap?
How are the 1991-2017 migration intervals, net-flow signs, route directions, negative rates, and the final non-five-year interval handled?
Does the country-language migration update run synchronously, and what guard prevents total outflow from exceeding an origin stock?
What exact cost function, parameter vector, initialization, learning rate, bounds, scaling, convergence criterion, fitted values, and residuals reproduce the forecasts?
What numerical arrays underlie Figures 3-10, and how do worldwide and summed country-language forecasts reconcile?
What are the ANOVA groups, replicates, assumptions, degrees of freedom, significance level, and multiple-testing correction for Tables A3-A7?
What unit and employee-count interpretation makes Q_i(n)/P_i times F minus Cn dimensionally valid?
What city-specific revenue, salary, hiring, communication, technology, existing-office, switching, and budget data would reproduce the office decision?
What random seed, swap distribution, perturbation magnitudes, and joint scenarios support the sensitivity statements?
Which future observations and error thresholds would count as successful external validation?
